name: The Hall of Letters
goal: Manipulate text by index, slice and method, and know why strings cannot be edited in place.

description.what: How Python lets you reach into a piece of text: one character at a time by position, a run of characters at a time by slice, whole transformations at a time by method, and a finished line of output built from values you already hold.
description.why: Almost everything a program is given by a person, a file or another program arrives as text, and almost nothing useful can be done with it until it has been cut apart, cleaned up and rebuilt into the shape the next step needs.
description.enables: You will be able to pull a character or a run of characters out of any text by position, count from either end, reshape text with the built-in methods, and compose a formatted line from names and numbers without a chain of `+` and `str`.
description.assumes: You can write a function with parameters and a return value, break a problem into functions, write a loop and an `if`, and call `len` on a piece of text.
description.assessed: You will predict what indexing, slicing and method calls produce, repair a function that tries to edit a character in place, and write functions that take text apart and rebuild it, with the later prompts telling you only what the result must be.

sections.title: Counting From Zero, and From the End
sections.body:
A piece of text is a run of characters with an order, and each character has a **position** - Python calls it an **index**. The first character is at index `0`, not `1`, so in `"ansuz"` the letter `a` is at 0, `n` at 1, `s` at 2, `u` at 3 and `z` at 4. Square brackets ask for one character by index: `rune[i]` hands back the single character sitting at position `i`, as a piece of text one character long.

Because the counting starts at zero, the last index of a text of length 5 is 4, never 5. Asking for `rune[5]` raises `IndexError: string index out of range` - the same kind of failure you learnt to read on the reading-failure floor, and it is telling the truth rather than being fussy.

A **negative** index counts backwards from the end: `-1` is the last character, `-2` the one before it. This is worth more than it looks, because the last character of text whose length you do not know is `text[-1]` and nothing else needs working out.

`len(text)` gives the number of characters, so the last index is always `len(text) - 1`. Those two facts together - zero at the front, `len - 1` at the back - are the whole of indexing.
sections.code:
rune = "ansuz"
i = 0
print(rune[i])
print(rune[i + 3])
print(rune[-1])
print(rune[-2])
print(len(rune))

annotations.text: `i` is 0, so this is the first character. Positions are ordinary numbers: they can be held under a name and worked out.
`-1` is the last character, whatever the length happens to be. Counting backwards never needs `len` at all.
Five characters, so the valid indexes run 0 to 4. Asking for index 5 would raise IndexError.

checkpoint.prompt: Fill the blanks so the program prints `c` on the first line and `n` on the second. Count forwards for the first and backwards for the second.
checkpoint.explain: The first character sits at 0 rather than 1, and the last at -1 rather than at the length. Writing 1 in the first blank prints `a`, which is the commonest slip in the language and never announces itself as an error.

sections.title: Slices, and the Half-Open Interval
sections.body:
One character at a time is rarely what you want. `word[start:stop]` hands back a whole run of characters as a **new** piece of text - a **slice**.

The rule that catches everybody: a slice **includes** `start` and **excludes** `stop`. So a slice that stops at 4 gives you characters 0, 1, 2 and 3 and no more. This is exactly the convention `range(0, 4)` uses on the repetition floor, and it is deliberate. It buys two things: the length of the slice is always `stop - start`, and two adjacent slices join back up perfectly, dropping nothing and repeating nothing.

Either end may be left out. `word[:cut]` means from the beginning, `word[cut:]` means to the end, and `word[:]` means all of it. Negative numbers work here too, so `word[-3:]` is the last three characters however long the word is.

A third number is the **step**: `word[::-1]` walks the whole thing backwards, which is how text gets reversed. One more difference from indexing: a slice never raises for being out of range. It hands back whatever is really there, which may be nothing at all.
sections.code:
word = "grimoire"
cut = 4
print(word[:cut])
print(word[cut:])
print(word[-3:])
print(word[cut - 3:cut])
print(word[::-1])
print(word[:cut] + word[cut:])

annotations.text: From the beginning up to but not including index 4 - four characters, because 4 - 0 = 4.
From index 4 to the end. The same number is the stop above and the start here, and the two slices meet exactly.
A step of -1 walks backwards through the whole text. Nothing was reversed in place: this builds a second piece of text.
The two halves added back together are the original word, which is the half-open interval paying for itself.

checkpoint.prompt: Fill the two blanks so the program prints `moir`.
checkpoint.explain: `m` sits at index 3 and `r` at index 6, so the stop must be 7 - one past the last character wanted. Writing 6 is the usual slip and it gives `moi` in silence rather than raising, which is why the half-open interval has to be understood rather than guessed at.

sections.title: Methods Hand Back a New String
sections.body:
A **method** is a function that belongs to a value and is called with a dot: `text.upper()`. The ones worth knowing now are `upper`, `lower`, `title` and `capitalize` for case, `strip` for blank space at the ends, `replace` for swapping one run of characters for another, `find` for the index where something first appears and `-1` when it never does, `count` for how many times it appears, and `startswith` and `endswith` for yes-or-no questions about the ends.

Every one of them **returns a new piece of text and leaves the original exactly as it was**. `name.strip()` on a line of its own is not a mistake Python will report; it quietly builds the stripped text and throws it away. What you want is almost always `name = name.strip()`.

That is not an accident of the library. A string in Python is **immutable**: once it exists it cannot be altered. There is no method anywhere that edits text in place, and writing `word[0] = "A"` fails with `TypeError: 'str' object does not support item assignment`.

So the way to change text is to build the text you want out of the pieces you have - a slice, a method result, a `+` - and to give the result a name. Rebuilding, never editing.
sections.code:
name = "  merlin  "
tidy = name.strip()
print(tidy)
print(tidy.upper(), tidy.capitalize())
print(tidy.replace("m", "M"))
print(tidy.find("l"), tidy.count("l"))
print(name.strip() == tidy, len(name))

annotations.text: The result of `strip` is kept under a name. Without that assignment the tidied text would exist for an instant and vanish.
`replace` swaps every appearance, not merely the first, and hands back a new string. `tidy` is untouched by it.
`name` still carries its blank space: the original was never modified, only read. Its length proves it.

checkpoint.code:
title = "The Grey Tome"
title.lower()
print(title)
print(title.lower().replace(" ", ""))
checkpoint.explain: The second line builds a lower-case copy that nothing catches, so `title` is unchanged when it is printed. The tempting reading is that a method call is a command that alters the value; it is an expression that produces a new one.

sections.title: Building a Line With f-strings
sections.body:
Gluing text and numbers together with `+` needs a `str()` around every number and quickly turns into a wall of quotation marks. An **f-string** does the same job by putting the values inside the text. Write `f` immediately before the opening quote, and anything inside `{ }` is worked out and dropped into place.

What goes inside the braces is a full expression, not merely a name: `f"{name.upper()}"`, `f"{len(name)}"` and `f"{level * cost}"` are all fine. Numbers are converted for you, so `str()` disappears from your code.

A colon inside the braces adds formatting. `{value:.2f}` shows a number with exactly two decimal places, which is what money needs: `2.5` prints as `2.50` rather than `2.5`.

An f-string is an ordinary piece of text once it is built, so it can be returned from a function, stored under a name or printed - and, like every other string, it cannot be edited afterwards.
sections.code:
name = "elara"
level = 7
cost = 2.5
print(name + " is level " + str(level))
print(f"{name} is level {level}")
print(f"{name.upper()} pays {level * cost:.2f} mana")
print(f"{name.title()} has {len(name)} letters")

annotations.text: The long way round: every number needs `str()`, and one forgotten one raises TypeError.
The same line as an f-string. The `f` before the quote is what makes the braces mean anything at all.
An expression inside the braces, and `.2f` fixing the result at two decimal places.

checkpoint.code:
gem = "opal"
count = 3
price = 2.5
print(f"{count} x {gem} = {count * price:.2f}")
print(f"{gem.upper()}!")
checkpoint.explain: `.2f` pads 7.5 out to two decimal places, so the answer is not `7.5`. The second line shows that a method call inside the braces is worked out before the line is built, and that the exclamation mark outside them is ordinary text.

guided-practice.code:
rune = "ansuz"
print(rune[-1] + rune[-5])
i = 2
print(rune[i])
print(len(rune))
guided-practice.explain: Two single characters added together make a two-character piece of text rather than a sum, because `+` between text joins it. The second print is the one that catches people: index 2 is the third character, because the counting began at zero.
guided-practice.hint: Write the indexes above the letters: a is 0, n is 1, s is 2, u is 3, z is 4. Then count backwards as well: z is -1, u is -2, s is -3, n is -4, a is -5.

guided-practice.prompt: Fill the blanks so the program prints `cant` on the first line and `ation` on the second.
guided-practice.explain: The same number 6 does two different jobs here: as a stop it is one past the last character taken, and as a start it is the first character taken. That is the half-open interval in a single program - the two slices meet at 6 and neither drop nor repeat a character.
guided-practice.hint: Number the letters from zero: i0 n1 c2 a3 n4 t5 a6 t7 i8 o9 n10. The stop index is excluded.

guided-practice.code:
motto = "Speak Softly"
motto.lower()
print(motto)
print(motto.lower())
print(motto.replace(" ", ""))
print(motto)
guided-practice.answer:
Speak Softly
speak softly
SpeakSoftly
Speak Softly
guided-practice.explain: Line 2 and line 5 both build new text that nothing keeps, so `motto` is identical on the first and the last line of output. The tempting reading is that a method call changes the value it is called on; it does not, and cannot, because that value is immutable.
guided-practice.hint: Ask of every method call: was the result stored anywhere, or printed? If neither, it changed nothing at all.

guided-practice.prompt:
`capitalise_first(word)` should hand back the word with its first character in upper case and every other character untouched, and empty text unchanged.

As written it fails with `TypeError: 'str' object does not support item assignment` - it is trying to write a new character into the word it was given. Repair it so that it builds the answer instead.
guided-practice.starterCode:
def capitalise_first(word):
    cut = 1
    word[:cut] = word[:cut].upper()
    return word
guided-practice.hint: Nothing can be written into a string. Build the answer from two pieces - the first character in upper case, and everything from the second character onwards - and return that.
guided-practice.explain: Empty text is the case that decides the shape: indexing the first character would raise IndexError on it, while a slice of empty text is simply empty and the `+` gives back nothing at all. The tempting repair is to reach for a method that upper-cases in place, and there is none, because immutability means every change is a new value.

guided-practice.prompt:
Write `middle(text)`, which returns the single character sitting exactly in the middle of `text`. You may assume the length of `text` is an odd number of at least one.

For `"abc"` the answer is `"b"`.
guided-practice.hint: For text of length 7 the middle index is 3, and for length 1 it is 0. Whole-number division by 2 gives exactly that, and the result goes inside the square brackets.
guided-practice.explain: Whole-number division is what makes this work: for length 7 there are three characters either side of index 3, and `7 // 2` is 3 rather than 3.5. Using `/` instead gives a float, and a float in square brackets raises TypeError - a position is counted, never measured.

guided-practice.prompt: Write `mirror(text)`, which returns `text` followed immediately by the same text backwards. `"grim"` becomes `"grimmirg"`, and empty text stays empty.
guided-practice.hint: Leave both ends of the slice out and give it a step of -1. Then join the original and the backwards copy with `+`.
guided-practice.explain: A step of -1 with both ends left out is the whole text walked from the back, and it costs one slice rather than a loop with a counter. Notice that nothing was reversed: `text` is exactly as it was, and a second, separate piece of text was built beside it.

guided-practice.prompt:
Write `tidy(name)`, which returns `name` with blank space removed from both ends, its first character in upper case and every other character in lower case.

`"  MERLIN "` becomes `"Merlin"`, and text that is nothing but blank space becomes empty text.
guided-practice.hint: `strip` hands back a new string, so the case method has to be called on that result rather than on the original. Two calls chain with a second dot.
guided-practice.explain: The last test is the honest one: the method that fixes the first character also forces everything after it into lower case, so `pERCival` becomes `percival` and not `Percival`. It is one method with one behaviour, not a general title-caser, and choosing it means accepting what it does to the rest of the text.

guided-practice.prompt:
Write `badge(name, level, mana)`, which returns a single line of exactly this shape:

`ELARA (level 7) 3.50 mana`

The name is shown in upper case, the level exactly as given, and the mana always with two decimal places.
guided-practice.solution:
def badge(name, level, mana):
    return f"{name.upper()} (level {level}) {mana:.2f} mana"
guided-practice.hint: Put an `f` before the opening quote and write the fixed text out as it should appear, with each value in braces. Two decimal places is `{mana:.2f}`.
guided-practice.explain: The whole number 0 has to come out as `0.00`, which is what the `.2f` is for - without it a whole number prints with no decimal point at all, so the line is wrong for exactly the values a test is most likely to try. The empty name is a reminder that the braces drop in whatever is there, including nothing, and the spacing around them is ordinary text either way.

independent-practice.prompt:
Write `initials(full_name)`. A name arrives as exactly two words with a single space between them. Return the two initials in upper case, each followed by a full stop.

`"ada lovelace"` gives `"A.L."`
independent-practice.solution:
def initials(full_name):
    gap = full_name.find(" ")
    first = full_name[:gap]
    second = full_name[gap + 1:]
    return first[:1].upper() + "." + second[:1].upper() + "."
independent-practice.explain: Everything turns on locating the space, because the second word begins one position after it and at no fixed index. `"x y"` is the case that punishes a hard-coded position: it comes out right only if the second initial is found relative to the gap rather than at index 2 by luck.

independent-practice.prompt:
Write `redact(text, secret)`. Every appearance of `secret` inside `text` must come back as a run of asterisks of exactly the same length, and everything else must be untouched.

`redact("the code is swordfish", "swordfish")` gives `"the code is *********"`. You may assume `secret` is not empty.
independent-practice.solution:
def redact(text, secret):
    return text.replace(secret, "*" * len(secret))
independent-practice.explain: `*` between a piece of text and a number repeats that text, which is how a mask of the right length is built without counting anything by hand. The second case is the one that catches an answer assuming the secret is present: the swap must simply do nothing when there is nothing to swap, and it does.

independent-practice.prompt:
Write `is_palindrome(text)`, returning `True` when `text` reads the same forwards and backwards once spaces are ignored and upper and lower case count as the same, and `False` otherwise. Empty text counts as a palindrome.

`"A man a plan a canal Panama"` is `True`.

tests.input: 'A man a plan a canal Panama'

independent-practice.explain: The cleaning has to happen before the comparison, because comparing `"A man a plan"` with itself backwards fails on the capital letter and the spaces long before the letters disagree. Building a cleaned copy is the only option available: text cannot be edited in place, so the tidied version has to live somewhere new.

independent-practice.prompt:
Write `tail(text, mark)`. `mark` is a single character. Return everything that comes after the last appearance of `mark` in `text`, and the whole of `text` when `mark` never appears at all.

`tail("chapter/one/rune", "/")` gives `"rune"`.
independent-practice.explain: Searching from the left gives `"one/rune"` for the first case, so the direction of the search is the whole problem. There is a small piece of luck worth noticing rather than depending on: a failed search reports -1, and one past -1 is 0, so the missing-mark case falls out of the same expression instead of needing its own branch.

independent-practice.prompt:
Write `receipt_line(item, count, price)`, which returns one line of exactly this shape:

`candle x3 = 13.50`

The number after the `x` is the count, and the amount at the end is the count times the price, always shown with two decimal places.
independent-practice.solution:
def receipt_line(item, count, price):
    return f"{item} x{count} = {count * price:.2f}"
independent-practice.explain: The last case shows that two decimal places is a rounding of the true total rather than a truncation of it: 6.666 is reported as 6.67. A count of zero is the other edge worth having, because a total of nothing must still be shown as `0.00` if the line is to sit squarely under every other line on the receipt.

independent-practice.prompt:
Write `shorten(text, limit)`. When `text` is no longer than `limit` characters, return it exactly as it is. When it is longer, return its first `limit` characters with `...` on the end.

`shorten("grimoire", 4)` gives `"grim..."`.
independent-practice.explain: Text of exactly `limit` characters has to come back untouched, which is why the comparison must allow equality - `<` in place of `<=` hangs a needless `...` on text that fitted perfectly. A limit of 0 is the other end of the same idea: the cut is empty and the marker is all that survives.

exam.prompt: A Python string is **immutable**. Which of these is what that word means?
choices: Once a string exists, no operation can alter it; every change produces a new string.
A string cannot be passed to a function, only copied into one.
A string cannot be compared with another string using `==`.
A string cannot contain a character that already appears in it.
exam.explain: Immutability is a fact about the value, not about what may be done with a name: `name = name.upper()` is perfectly legal because it points the name at a new string, while `name[0] = "A"` is not, because it asks the existing string to change. The second option is the usual confusion, mixing immutability up with how arguments are passed.

exam.prompt: In the slice `text[2:5]`, which positions of `text` end up in the result?
exam.explain: The interval is half-open: the start is included and the stop excluded, so three characters come back and the length is 5 - 2. The second option is the natural reading of English rather than of Python, and this is the same convention `range(2, 5)` uses, which is why the two were taught as one idea.

exam.code:
word = "grimoire"
cut = 4
print(word[:cut])
print(word[cut:])
print(word[-3:])
print(word[::-1])
print(word[cut:cut] + "!")
exam.explain: The last line is the one to think about: a slice whose start and stop are the same is empty rather than one character long, and it does not raise. That forgiveness is the difference between slicing and indexing, and it is why a slice is the safer tool when the numbers are worked out rather than typed.

exam.code:
name = "elara"
mana = 7
cost = 2.5
print(f"{name.title()} has {mana} mana")
print(f"{name.upper()}: {mana * cost:.2f}")
print(f"{len(name)} letters, last is {name[-1]}")
exam.answer:
Elara has 7 mana
ELARA: 17.50
5 letters, last is a
exam.explain: Braces hold whole expressions, so the method call, the multiplication and the `len` are all worked out before the line is built. The `.2f` turns 17.5 into `17.50`, which is the detail most people leave out when predicting this by eye.

exam.prompt: Fill the blanks with method names so the program prints `fire bolt` with no blank space at either end. The first blank takes no arguments; the second takes the two shown.
exam.explain: Each method hands back a new string, which is exactly what lets the next dot attach to the result rather than to the original. A chain reads left to right in the order the work happens, and neither call touches `spell` itself.

exam.prompt: Put these lines in order to make a working `initial_dot(name)` that returns the first character of a name in upper case followed by a full stop, and empty text when the name is nothing but blank space.
exam.explain: The guard has to sit after the tidying and before the slicing, because it is the tidied text that might be empty and a name of pure blank space is not empty until it has been stripped. Testing `name` instead of `tidy` would let three spaces walk straight through to the end.

exam.prompt: A colleague's function begins with the line `name.strip()` and they cannot work out why the leading spaces are still there afterwards. Explain what that line actually does, what becomes of its result, and what they should have written instead.
exam.explain: The line is not wrong so much as pointless: it builds the stripped text correctly and then throws it away, because nothing catches the result. This is the everyday consequence of immutability, and `name = name.strip()` is the fix - the same shape that every method on this floor needs.

exam.prompt:
Write `slugify(title)`, which returns `title` with blank space removed from both ends, every letter in lower case, and each remaining space turned into a hyphen. You may assume the words inside the title are separated by exactly one space.

`"  The Grey Tome "` gives `"the-grey-tome"`.
exam.hint: Three method calls, chained: one for the ends, one for the case, one for the spaces. The order of the first two does not matter, but the stripping must happen before the spaces are swapped.
exam.explain: Swapping the spaces before stripping the ends is the trap: the outer spaces would become hyphens and the answer would be `-the-grey-tome-`. Chaining works at all only because each call hands back a new string for the next one to work on, which is immutability being useful rather than awkward.

exam.prompt:
Write `initial_and_surname(full_name)`. The name arrives as exactly two words with a single space between them. Return the first initial in upper case, a full stop, a space, then the surname with its first character in upper case and the rest of it as it was.

`"ada lovelace"` gives `"A. Lovelace"`.
exam.solution:
def initial_and_surname(full_name):
    cut = 1
    gap = full_name.find(" ")
    first = full_name[:gap]
    surname = full_name[gap + 1:]
    return first[:cut].upper() + ". " + surname[:cut].upper() + surname[cut:]
exam.hint: Find the space first: the surname starts one position after it. The surname is then its first character upper-cased, joined to everything from its second character onwards.
exam.explain: The last case decides whether the surname was upper-cased wholesale or one character at the front: only the first is touched, so `turing` becomes `Turing` while `ALAN` contributes nothing but its `A`. A surname of one character is the other edge, and it survives because the rest of it is an empty slice rather than an error.

exam.prompt:
`between(text, start, stop)` should return the characters of `text` from position `start` up to but not including position `stop`, so `between("grimoire", 0, 4)` is `"grim"`.

It is returning one character too few. Repair it.
exam.starterCode:
def between(text, start, stop):
    return text[start:stop - 1]
exam.solution:
def between(text, start, stop):
    return text[start:stop]
exam.hint: The stop of a slice is already excluded. Ask what the extra subtraction is correcting for, and whether anything needed correcting.
exam.explain: The subtraction was written by somebody guarding against an off-by-one that Python had already handled: the stop is excluded by the language, so taking one more away excludes two. The third case is where the mistaken version becomes visibly absurd rather than merely short, since an empty range turns into a backwards one.
